topic: What If You Could Jump on Every World in the Solar System?
title: WHAT IF YOU JUMPED
ON EVERY WORLD?

chapters.title: Mercury
card: SAME PULL AS MARS · 4,222 h DAY

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 0 cold open on a comet + title card
script.text: Pitch black space. Dusty rock under your sneakers. You crouch for a normal hop, push off, and keep rising. Higher and higher. The comet shrinks below your feet. Jump here and you never come back down. From worlds that launch you over houses to worlds that flatten you instantly: what if you jumped on every world?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Start with your Earth baseline. Stand in your school gym, crouch, and pop up beside the chalk wall. Slap! About half a metre. Outside in a floodlit stadium sits the high jump world record: two point four five metres, set by Javier Sotomayor in nineteen ninety three. Even the best human barely clears a doorway. Unless we leave Earth.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Step onto your bathroom scale, because a single rule runs this whole tour. Your leg muscles pack the same push everywhere. Only gravity changes. Less gravity means a higher jump and a longer hang time. More gravity drags you straight down. Ready to test that rule? Look out your window tonight.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Touch down on the Moon under a starry sky with blue Earth overhead. Lunar gravity pulls at about one point six two metres per second squared. Push off with your gym hop and boing! You soar about three metres high, floating for nearly four seconds before drifting softly into the grey dust. Wait: why did real astronauts barely hop?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Time for an Apollo reality check. Real astronauts wore stiff bulky spacesuits and heavy life support backpacks. Bending their knees felt like wrestling a giant mattress, so they jumped far less than our no suit leap. In nineteen seventy two, Charlie Duke tried a big high jump, tipped backwards in slow motion, and fell flat onto his backpack! Next stop: grab a basketball.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Welcome to the rusty red court of Mars, where gravity sits at about three point seven one metres per second squared. Dribble through red dust, plant your sneakers, and launch. You rise about two point six times higher than on Earth, gliding above the rim for an easy slam dunk! Want that exact same bounce somewhere way stranger? Head toward the Sun.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 6 Mercury: same pull as Mars, 4,222 h solar day
script.text: Cratered Mercury looks tiny, yet its dense core gives it basically the same gravity pull as Mars. You leap just as high over silver rock. Then you unfold a chair to watch the sunrise before jumping again. You wait. And you wait. A solar day on Mercury lasts about four thousand, two hundred and twenty two hours. Pack snacks, because the next planet cooks them.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Drop beneath the yellow clouds of Venus and forget jumping altogether. Thick air crushes down at about ninety three times Earth's surface pressure, like being about nine hundred metres underwater without a submarine. Worse, the rocks bake at about four hundred and sixty five degrees Celsius. You do not jump here: you get squished like a panini and cooked! Could a robot survive?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Engineers tried. Tough Soviet Venera probes parachuted down inside heavy titanium shells just to photograph that glowing landscape. The moment a lander touched the ground, a brutal countdown clock started. Tick, tick, sizzle. Even the longest lasting Soviet probe survived only about two hours on the surface before Venus fried it silent. Let us cool off somewhere thick air actually helps.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 9 Titan cardboard wings: ~4x air density, ~1/7 gravity
script.text: Out around Saturn orbits hazy golden Titan. Gravity here pulls at only about one seventh of Earth's, while the cold surface air is about four times denser than ours. Tape cardboard wings to your arms, hop off an icy boulder, and flap hard! Those homemade wings catch the soupy air and lift you airborne above dark lakes. Feeling unstoppable? Try Jupiter.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 10 Jupiter diving board: no surface, ~2.5x gravity, 70 kg -> ~165 kg, ~20 cm jump, sink
script.text: Bad news: giant striped Jupiter has no solid surface at all, so we hang a diving board in its upper clouds. At about two point five times Earth's gravity, your knees groan. A seventy kilogram you weighs like about one hundred and sixty five kilograms on Earth. You strain, hop about twenty centimetres, land, and sink straight into the clouds! At least the next giant floats.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 11 Saturn in a giant bathtub: 687 kg/m^3
script.text: Ringed Saturn has no solid floor either, though near its clouds your weight feels close to home. Instead, Saturn hides a wild party trick. On average, it has a density of about six hundred and eighty seven kilograms per cubic metre, less dense than water! Fill a giant bathtub, drop Saturn in beside a rubber duck, and the planet floats. Now grab a bowling ball.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 12 Bowling alley: Uranus ~98 deg tilt, Neptune pulls harder than Earth
script.text: Step into the outer solar system's ice giant bowling alley. Down the left lane rolls pale cyan Uranus, spinning tipped right over on its side at about ninety eight degrees like a tumbling barrel. Hop near its clouds and you bounce slightly easier than home. Try deep blue Neptune next door, though, and oof: Neptune pulls a bit harder than Earth. Ready for superhero mode?

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 13 Pluto: 0.62 m/s^2, ~7 m high, ~9 s airtime, 70 kg -> ~4-5 kg
script.text: Land on icy Pluto, where the Sun shrinks to a bright star over a heart shaped glacier. Gravity drops to about zero point six two metres per second squared, so a seventy kilogram you weighs like about four to five kilograms on Earth. Push off and you rocket about seven metres high, clearing a house with roughly nine seconds of airtime! Tiny worlds get wilder still.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 14 Dimorphos: ~151 m wide, DART 2022 shortened orbit ~33 min
script.text: Tiptoe onto Dimorphos, a rubble asteroid only about one hundred and fifty one metres wide. It is so small NASA used it for target practice: in twenty twenty two, the DART spacecraft slammed into Dimorphos and shortened its orbit by about thirty three minutes. Gravity here barely whispers. Even a tiny flinch sends you floating up, leading straight back to where we started.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 15 Comet payoff: ESA Philae on 67P bounced ~38 cm/s, ~1 km, ~2 hours
script.text: Remember our opening comet? When the European Space Agency set its Philae lander onto comet sixty seven P, its harpoons failed. Philae bounced off at about thirty eight centimetres per second, slower than a stroll, yet flew for about one kilometre over nearly two hours! Your jump is much faster than that bounce. Push off here, wave goodbye, and off you go into space forever.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 16 The Sun: ~28x Earth gravity, couldn't stand
script.text: Final boss: the Sun. Give yourself magic heat proof boots and an imaginary platform at the solar surface. Solar gravity slams down at about twenty eight times Earth's pull. Forget jumping: you could not even stand! Your knees buckle, your face pancakes onto the deck, and wiggling a thumb feels heroic. Suddenly, ordinary Earth sounds pretty wonderful.

script.speaker: narrator
script.beat: 17 Rooftop at dawn: 0.5m feels perfect, Mars+Jupiter mid-Nov, Leonids 17-18 Nov, CTA
script.text: Back on your city rooftop at dawn, take a little hop. About half a metre up, soft thud down. Your tiny Earth jump suddenly feels perfect. And you can spot part of this tour yourself: Mars and Jupiter appear very close together in the mid November sky, and the Leonid meteors peak around the seventeenth and eighteenth of November, so look up. Which world would you jump on first?

science.claim: Baseline standing vertical jump on Earth is about 0.5 m (no spacesuit); the men's high-jump world record is 2.45 m set by Javier Sotomayor in 1993.
science.working: 0.5 m is the illustrative standing-jump baseline assumption (take-off speed v0 = sqrt(2 * g_Earth * 0.5) ≈ 3.13 m/s). Javier Sotomayor cleared 2.45 m in Salamanca on 27 July 1993.
science.source: Illustrative physics baseline (0.5 m); World Athletics world records (2.45 m, Javier Sotomayor, 1993)

science.claim: Less gravity produces a proportionally higher jump and longer hang time for the same leg push.
science.working: With constant take-off velocity v0, peak height h = v0^2 / (2g) scales as 1/g, and total hang time T = 2*v0 / g also scales as 1/g.
science.source: Newtonian projectile kinematics; NASA Planetary Fact Sheets

science.claim: On the Moon (gravity 1.62 m/s²), a 0.5 m Earth jump reaches about 3 m high and lasts nearly 4 seconds.
Real Apollo astronauts in stiff pressurized spacesuits jumped far lower; in 1972 Charlie Duke fell over backwards attempting a lunar high jump.
science.working: During Apollo 16 EVA-3 (April 1972), astronaut Charlie Duke jumped near the Lunar Module, lost balance due to his heavy PLSS backpack, and fell backwards onto the pack without breaching the suit.

science.claim: On Mars (gravity 3.71 m/s²), you jump about 2.6x higher than on Earth; Mercury has nearly the same surface gravity pull as Mars, with a solar day lasting about 4,222 hours.
science.working: g_Earth / g_Mars = 9.81 / 3.71 ≈ 2.64 (about 2.6x). NASA Planetary Fact Sheet lists Mercury surface gravity at 3.7 m/s² (same pull as Mars) and length of solar day at 4,222.6 hours (about 4,222 hours).
science.source: NASA Mars Fact Sheet; NASA Mercury Fact Sheet

science.claim: Venus has a surface pressure about 93x Earth's (like being about 900 m underwater) and a surface temperature of about 465 °C; the longest-lasting Soviet Venera probe survived about 2 hours on the surface.
science.working: 93 bar atmospheric pressure corresponds to hydrostatic water depth ~900 m; mean surface temperature ~465 °C. Soviet lander Venera 13 transmitted for 127 minutes (about 2 hours) in 1982.
science.source: NASA Venus Fact Sheet and NASA Science Venus Facts

science.claim: Saturn's moon Titan has surface air about 4x denser than Earth's and surface gravity about 1/7 of Earth's, allowing human-powered winged flight.
science.working: Titan surface gravity ≈ 1.35 m/s² (≈ 1/7 Earth's) and dense nitrogen atmosphere (~1.5 bar at ~94 K) yields ~4x Earth's sea-level air density, drastically reducing stall speed and power needed to flap wings.
science.source: NASA Titan / Dragonfly Mission Science Fact Sheet

science.claim: Jupiter has no solid surface; at about 2.5x Earth's gravity near its cloud tops, a 70 kg person weighs like about 165 kg on Earth and a 0.5 m jump shrinks to about 20 cm.
science.working: NASA Jupiter Fact Sheet (1-bar cloud level gravity ~23.1–24.8 m/s², ~2.4–2.5x Earth): 70 kg * (23.1 / 9.8) ≈ 165 kg equivalent weight; 0.5 m / 2.5 = 0.20 m (20 cm).

science.claim: Saturn has an average bulk density of 687 kg/m³, less dense than liquid water.
science.working: Mean density of Saturn = 687 kg/m³ < 1,000 kg/m³ (water), so its bulk density is lower than water.

science.claim: Uranus spins tipped over on its side at about 98 degrees, while Neptune pulls a bit harder than Earth.
science.working: Uranus obliquity to orbit = 97.77° (about 98°), cloud-top gravity 8.7 m/s² (< Earth); Neptune cloud-top gravity 11.0 m/s² (> Earth).
science.source: NASA Uranus Fact Sheet; NASA Neptune Fact Sheet

science.claim: On Pluto (gravity 0.62 m/s²), a jump reaches about 7 m high with roughly 9 seconds of airtime, and a 70 kg person weighs like about 4–5 kg on Earth.
science.working: At g = 0.62–0.7 m/s², jump height is ~7 m and hang time ~9 s; 70 kg * (0.62 / 9.81) ≈ 4.4 kg (about 4–5 kg).

science.claim: Asteroid Dimorphos is about 151 m wide; NASA's DART spacecraft hit it in 2022 and shortened its orbit by about 33 minutes.
science.working: DART impacted the ~151 m moonlet Dimorphos on 26 September 2022, reducing its 11 h 55 min binary orbit around Didymos by ~33 minutes.
science.source: NASA DART / ESA Hera Mission Fact Sheets

science.claim: ESA's Philae lander bounced off comet 67P at about 38 cm/s and flew for about 1 km over nearly 2 hours; a human jump is much faster and escapes into space.
science.working: On 12 November 2014, Philae rebounded from 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko at ~38 cm/s (0.38 m/s), travelling ~1 km for 1 h 50 min (~2 hours). A human jump (~3.1 m/s) far exceeds both 0.38 m/s and 67P's ~0.5–1 m/s escape velocity.

science.claim: The Sun pulls at about 28x Earth's gravity, so you could not even stand.
science.working: Solar photospheric gravity ≈ 274 m/s² ≈ 27.9x (about 28x) Earth's gravity (no solid surface).

science.claim: Mars and Jupiter appear very close together in the sky in mid-November 2026, and the Leonid meteor shower peaks around 17–18 November 2026.
science.working: Pre-dawn conjunction of Mars and Jupiter in mid-November 2026 (15–16 Nov); Leonid meteor shower peaks overnight 17–18 November 2026.
science.source: NASA What's Up: November 2026; Royal Observatory Greenwich Leonid Meteor Shower 2026 Guide
